blocks.text: A covalent bond is formed by the mutual sharing of electrons between two atoms. While sharing electrons, each atom completes its valence shell and attains the nearest noble gas configuration. A covalent bond may be non-polar or polar in character. The bond between two chlorine atoms is purely covalent and non-polar: the electronegativity of the two atoms is exactly the same, so the bonded atoms remain electrically neutral and there is no charge on either atom. Other such molecules are H2, F2, Br2 and I2. Examples of polar covalent bonds are H-Cl, H-Br and the bonds in H2O.

blocks.alt: Shell diagrams of two chlorine atoms (2, 8, 7), one with electrons as crosses and one as dots. They overlap so that one electron from each is shared between them, ringed as the shared pair; each atom then has eight outer electrons in Cl2.
blocks.caption: Formation of a covalent bond between two Cl atoms (original diagram after Figure 3.2).

rows: Same electronegativity, no charge on either atom

blocks.prompt: Why is the bond in Br2 non-polar while the bond in H-Br is polar, although both are covalent?
blocks.explanation: In Br2 the two atoms are identical and have the same electronegativity, so the shared pair sits midway and neither atom carries a charge. In H-Br the bromine atom is more electronegative than hydrogen, pulls the shared pair towards itself, and the bond gains partial charges, which makes it polar.

items: Covalent bond: mutual sharing of electrons so each atom reaches a noble gas configuration; non-polar when the atoms have equal electronegativity (Cl2, H2, F2, Br2, I2), polar when they differ (H-Cl, H-Br, H2O).
